title: Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty in children: a systematic review of the literature
condition_or_topic: Robot-assisted laparoscopic pyeloplasty (RALP) for ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) in children
clinical_background: UPJO may result from narrowing of the proximal ureter or compression by aberrant lower-pole vessels. Prenatal screening has increased detection of hydronephrosis and lowered the age at which pyeloplasty is performed. Hydronephrosis is detected in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds, and approximately 25% of prenatally diagnosed UPJO cases require surgery. Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty remains the established treatment, with reported success rates of 90 to 100%. Laparoscopic pyeloplasty offers a minimally invasive alternative but poses challenges in suturing, ergonomics, and training. RALP has become the most commonly performed robotic procedure in pediatric urology, although its use in very small children remains a concern.
objectives: Review international literature published during 2012–2022 on RALP in patients with UPJO.
Examine surgical indications, success rates, complications, redo procedures, anatomically challenging cases, costs, training, learning curves, and future developments in pediatric RALP.
study_design: Systematic literature review of robotic-assisted pyeloplasty for pediatric UPJO. The authors searched PubMed for publications from 2012–2022 using combinations of terms concerning pediatric pyeloplasty, robotic surgery, cost, age, weight, simulation, and learning curves. They assessed articles for relevance and checked bibliographies for further citations; inclusion was based on their evaluation and interpretation.

population.description: Children with UPJO considered for robotic-assisted pyeloplasty.
inclusion_criteria: Literature published during 2012–2022 and relevant to robotic-assisted pyeloplasty in patients with UPJO, as judged by the authors.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that RALP is safe and effective for pediatric UPJO, including recurrent obstruction and anatomically complex cases. Instrument size limits its use in small children and infants, while cost remains a concern; the authors call for higher-quality studies, pediatric-specific technology, and structured training before RALP can attain gold-standard status.
narrative_summary:
This review examined literature on robotic-assisted pyeloplasty for children with UPJO published during 2012–2022. The authors searched PubMed and assessed relevant articles and their bibliographies. They report pediatric RALP success rates ranging from 90 to 100%. Compared with open or laparoscopic pyeloplasty, RALP is associated with shorter hospital stays and less postoperative pain medication; operative times have improved with experience. The review also describes RALP as an effective option for recurrent UPJO and complex anatomy. In a cited multicenter study of children with horseshoe kidney, the overall success rate was 92.8%.

The indications for RALP are described as the same as those for open or laparoscopic surgery. Use in small children and infants remains challenging because instrument size and restricted working space complicate port placement; although published findings in younger infants are encouraging, the studies are mostly retrospective. The authors also identify cost as a continuing limitation. Training findings cited in the review suggest that proficiency may be reached sooner with RALP than with laparoscopic pyeloplasty, but simulation alone is insufficient: the authors favor training that also includes mentorship. They recommend high-quality prospective observational studies and clinical trials in small children, a pediatric robotic curriculum, and pediatric-specific instruments and technology before RALP is regarded as the gold standard.
interpretation: The authors consider RALP a safe and effective option for children with UPJO, including recurrent obstruction and anatomically complex cases. They report pediatric success rates of 90 to 100% and describe shorter hospital stays and reduced postoperative pain-medication use compared with open or laparoscopic pyeloplasty. Operative times have improved with experience. Although the robotic approach is increasingly favored, the authors do not regard its status as a gold standard as established, particularly for small children and infants.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier reports cited by the authors found that laparoscopic pyeloplasty was effective but technically demanding, whereas RALP facilitated intracorporeal suturing. A cited prospective multicenter comparison found both transperitoneal and retroperitoneal RALP safe and effective; the retroperitoneal approach involved a shorter hospital stay but a longer operation when crossing vessels were present. Reports of redo procedures described success comparable to primary RALP, with shorter stays and fewer complications than redo open pyeloplasty. Published cost analyses differed in scope: basic analyses found similar costs for robotic and conventional laparoscopic pyeloplasty, while analyses accounting for training, maintenance and materials indicated higher costs for RALP than for other approaches. Studies cited on training reported proficiency after 13 RALP cases versus at least 18 LP cases, with further improvement after 37 cases; another study found RALP operative times became comparable to open surgery after 15–20 cases. The authors note that pediatric reports of simultaneous pyelolithotomy and pyeloplasty describe the combination as safe and feasible, despite EAU guidance favoring separate procedures.
clinical_implications: The indications for RALP are the same as those for open or laparoscopic surgery: symptomatic obstruction, urinary tract infections, an obstructive pattern on functional renal imaging and/or worsening differential renal function.

For the smallest infants, open surgery may retain advantages because of anesthetic duration and the size of robotic instruments. Reports in younger and lighter infants are encouraging, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective.

RALP can facilitate identification and treatment of crossing vessels, fibrosis and ureteral stricture during redo reconstruction. Complex renal anatomy calls for experienced dissection to avoid vascular injury.

Early postoperative complications described in the literature range from fever, pain and hematuria (Clavien I) to urinary tract infection or urinary leakage (Clavien ≥ 2), and stent migration, omental herniation or ileocecal volvulus (Clavien IIIb). Reported late complications are uncommon and mostly Clavien IIIb.

Stent-related complications and discomfort in smaller children and infants have prompted reports of stentless RALP, but larger cohorts and longer follow-up are needed before its outcomes are better established.
practice_implications: The authors state that the first postnatal US should take place more than 48 h after birth to avoid underestimating dilation; they also describe 99mTc-MAG3 as recommended for neonatal renography and for imaging kidneys when renal function is compromised.

The choice of surgical approach should be individualized according to the patient and the surgeon's preference. The authors identify no settled preference between transperitoneal and retroperitoneal RALP.
When operating in infants, place trocars as far apart as feasible if the ideal 3–5 cm separation cannot be achieved. Appropriate bed positioning and port placement may help provide working space.
For complex anatomy, the cited multicenter study recommended the Anderson–Hynes technique with da Vinci Xi, with particular care to preserve upper-moiety ureteral vascularity in lower-pole UPJO.
Training should combine simulation with mentorship; the authors state that simulation alone is insufficient for proficiency.
Proposed measures to reduce costs include greater robot utilization, shorter OR turnover and more efficient preoperative holding.
limitations: Evidence concerning RALP in younger and lighter infants comes predominantly from retrospective studies.
Reports of stentless RALP require confirmation in larger cohorts with longer follow-up.
Instrument size and restricted working space make robotic surgery difficult in small children and infants; the available 5 mm instruments also have a limited selection and technical drawbacks.
High costs remain a limitation of robotic surgery. Sharing equipment across specialties can constrain opportunities to acquire experience.
open_questions: There is no established consensus on whether transperitoneal or retroperitoneal RALP is preferable.
The need for trans-anastomotic urinary diversion during pyeloplasty remains under debate.
There is no consensus on the preferred approach after failed pyeloplasty.
The role of RALP in the smallest children, including the influence of body weight on outcomes, remains uncertain.
A standardized pediatric robotic curriculum and training protocol are not yet available.
future_directions: Conduct high-quality prospective observational studies and clinical trials of RALP, particularly in small children.
Develop a pediatric robotic curriculum and evaluate training and learning curves.
Develop instruments and technologies tailored to children, including improvements to 5 mm instruments or possible 3 mm instruments.
Investigate approaches using fewer incisions, potentially including single-port platforms, and assess possible applications of augmented reality and augmented intelligence.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Robotic pyeloplasty developed after open and laparoscopic treatment of pediatric ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO). Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty (RALP) is described as a new gold standard in pediatric minimally invasive surgery. This review searched PubMed for literature published during the last 10 years (2012–2022). The authors state that robotic pyeloplasty is becoming the preferred approach for children with UPJO except the smallest infants: open surgery can reduce the duration of general anesthesia in these patients, and robotic instrument size remains restrictive. Compared with laparoscopy, the robotic approach is reported to have shorter operative times and similar success rates, hospital stays, and complications. RALP is described as easier to perform than other open or minimally invasive approaches for redo pyeloplasty. According to the review, robotic surgery had become the most frequently used treatment modality for UPJO by 2009, and its use has continued to increase. The authors consider pediatric RALP safe and effective, including for repeat operations and difficult anatomy, and report that junior surgeons can attain expertise comparable to senior surgeons more quickly. Cost remains a concern. They advise further high-quality prospective observational studies, clinical trials, and pediatric-specific technologies before RALP attains gold-standard status.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: UPJO can result from intrinsic fibrosis or stenosis of the proximal ureter, or from extrinsic compression by aberrant lower-pole vessels. Prenatal hydronephrosis has been detected in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds, with UPJO accounting for up to 41% of cases. A large proportion of presentations resembling UPJO, consisting of isolated hydronephrosis with or without calyceal dilation, are benign and resolve spontaneously; approximately 25% of prenatally diagnosed UPJO cases require surgery. Earlier diagnosis has significantly lowered the age at pyeloplasty. Since Anderson and Hynes first described their operation in 1949, surgeons have sought to simplify it and reduce complications. Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty, traditionally performed through an open flank incision, remains the gold standard for UPJ obstruction and has an overall success rate of 90 to 100%. Pediatric laparoscopic pyeloplasty (LP) was first reported in 1995 and was subsequently established as a safe and effective minimally invasive alternative. Its intracorporeal suturing and knotting, ergonomics, and learning curve remain challenging, and its general use in children was limited. After the da Vinci system became available in 2002, the first RALP series was assessed. Robotic surgery for children has advanced throughout the last 10 years; RALP has become the most commonly performed pediatric robotic urology operation, with reported success rates of 95%–100%. This review addresses indications, success, complications, repeat surgery, anatomically challenging cases, costs, training, the learning curve, and the future of robotic treatment for pediatric UPJO.

document_sections.heading: Material and methods
document_sections.content: The authors reviewed international literature from the past 10 years, 2012–2022, concerning robotic-assisted pyeloplasty in patients with UPJO. They searched PubMed® using combinations of terms addressing pediatric UPJO, several forms of pediatric robotic pyeloplasty, robotic surgery costs and cost analysis, the pediatric robotic learning curve and simulation, patient weight and age, and future pediatric robotic surgery. They assessed retrieved articles for relevance and examined their bibliographies for further citations. Inclusion depended on the authors’ evaluation, analysis, and interpretation.

document_sections.heading: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO)
document_sections.content: Prenatal screening ultrasonography (US) and postnatal imaging have increased detection of hydronephrosis and lowered the age at pyeloplasty. Prenatal hydronephrosis is identified in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds; UPJO occurs in 1 per 1000–2000 newborns. UPJO is more common in males, involves the left kidney in up to 67% of cases, and is bilateral in up to 10%. Urinary tract US assesses hydronephrosis severity, pelvocalyceal dilation, and renal cortical thinning at birth. In 1993, the Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) proposed a standardized US grade based on urinary tract dilation and parenchymal thickness. The urinary tract dilation (UTD) classification introduced in 2014 assesses six parameters: anterior–posterior renal pelvic diameter, urinary tract dilatation, parenchymal thickness, parenchymal appearance, ureteral status, and bladder status. The first postnatal US should occur more than 48 h after birth to avoid underestimating dilation. In addition to US, 99mTc-MAG3 is recommended for neonatal renography and visualization of kidneys when renal function is impaired. Functional immaturity of neonatal kidneys can produce increased residual cortical activity when the radiopharmaceutical and furosemide are administered together in an F0 study; activity may remain at up to 50% or more of its peak. This phenomenon resolves after the age of 3 months.

document_sections.heading: Indications
document_sections.content: RALP has the same indications as open or laparoscopic surgery: symptomatic obstruction, urinary tract infections, an obstructive pattern on functional renal scanning, and/or declining differential renal function (DRF). de Waard et al. speculated in 2018 that hypertension should also be considered an indication because relieving UPJO cures hypertension in most affected children. A cited study found comparable sex distribution, laterality, preoperative renal pelvis antero-posterior (AP) diameter, and affected-kidney split function between LP and RALP groups. Operating in very small spaces raises concerns, as do RALP’s relative value in small children and the effect of body weight on outcomes; no robotic devices have yet been developed exclusively for pediatric surgery. Although consensus favors a weight cutoff at 10–15 kg, some authors report successful robotic operations in infants and children under 1 year of age. Restricted space can complicate trocar placement and cause robotic-arm conflicts. A cited paper found that 5 mm rather than 8 mm instruments improve use of the available space, but monopolar curved scissors cannot be used through 5 mm ports, making monopolar hook diathermy the alternative. Correct bed position, reproducible ‘kite-like’ trocar placement, and a ‘tent effect’ appear sufficient to create working space and avoid prolonged setup and operative times regardless of weight. Findings in younger and lighter infants are encouraging, although the studies are mostly retrospective.

document_sections.heading: Surgical technique and operative time
document_sections.content: Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty is the preferred operation for UPJO. Most surgeons use a transperitoneal route, although some favor a retroperitoneal route. A cited prospective multicenter comparison found both transperitoneal and retroperitoneal RALP safe and effective; retroperitoneal RALP was associated with a shorter hospital stay but a longer operative time when crossing vessels were present. No single approach has achieved consensus, and selection remains a matter of surgeon preference. Port spacing of 3–5 cm is ideal, but when that is impractical in infants, trocars are placed as far apart as possible. Transabdominal RALP uses an infraumbilical robotic camera port; two 8 mm working ports on the midclavicular line, one epigastric port 2 cm below the subcostal arch and one in the right or left iliac fossa above the inguinal ligament; and one 5 mm assistant port between the camera and lower working port for left pyeloplasty, or between the camera and upper working port to elevate the liver for right pyeloplasty. Retroperitoneal port placement has also been standardized. Reports indicate that robot-assisted single-port laparoscopic pyeloplasty is feasible in pediatric patients who are not infants. The hidden incision endoscopic surgery (HIdES) technique seeks to avoid visible scars by positioning a robotic working port and the camera below the Pfannenstiel incision line and another working port infraumbilically. A cited cross-sectional comparison using da Vinci Xi Surgical System® found that three-port RALP offered success and safety similar to conventional fourport RALP, including in infants. The three-port method uses a percutaneous hitch stitch to support the renal pelvis and a 14-G angiocatheter inserted percutaneously for doubleJ stent placement. With accumulating experience, overall operative time (OT) has fallen; from 2019, most studies have reported an overall OT of less than 120 min. Whether trans-anastomotic ureteral stenting is necessary remains debated. Diversion is usually provided by an antegrade double-J stent or a cutaneous pyeloureteral (CPU) stent; the latter is intended to drain urine effectively, avoid secondary anesthesia and bleeding risks, and reduce costs. As RALP has expanded to smaller children and infants, whose stent-related complications and discomfort are more frequent, surgeons have begun performing stentless robotic pyeloplasty. Reported stent complications include migration, fragmentation, infection, fever, and pain. Reports of stentless RALP describe excellent success and few complications relative to conventional approaches, but larger cohorts and longer follow-up are needed.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: Reported pediatric RALP success rates range from 90 to 100%. Compared with open or laparoscopic pyeloplasty, RALP is associated with a shorter hospital stay and less postoperative pain medication. Its formerly longer operative times are improving, particularly where procedure volumes and surgeon experience are high. Early postoperative complications, occurring < 30 days, include fever, pain, and hematuria (Clavien I); urinary tract infection and mild or major urinary leaks (Clavien ≥ 2); and stent migration, omental herniation, and ileocecal volvulus (Clavien IIIb). Late complications, occurring ≥ 30 days, have been reported in few cases and were predominantly Clavien IIIb: ipsilateral ureteral stenosis, operations for umbilical hernia, J–J migration, urinary leakage, and stone formation.

document_sections.heading: Redo RALP
document_sections.content: Persistent or recurrent UPJO after an initial pyeloplasty occurs in 3 to 11% of cases, and there is no agreed gold-standard treatment after failure. The cited literature describes qualitative differences in reasons for secondary procedures: urine leaks occur more frequently after laparoscopic pyeloplasty, whereas complications associated with retrograde pyelogram (RPG) and stent placement occur after RALP; the authors suggest that easier intracorporeal suturing with RALP may explain this distinction. Repeat pyeloplasty is generally performed for obstruction caused by a crossing vessel, intrinsic narrowing, or high ureteral insertion. Patients often undergo unsuccessful endoscopic interventions, including stents, a percutaneous nephrostomy tube (PCN), endopyelotomy, or balloon dilation. RALP facilitates identification and simultaneous surgical treatment of crossing vessels. Recurrent obstruction is harder to manage because of scar tissue, fibrosis, and reduced ureteral vascularity, so its treatment is reserved for highly experienced surgeons. Nevertheless, redo RALP is considered safe and effective, with shorter hospitalization and fewer complications than repeat open pyeloplasty, and a high success rate comparable to primary RALP.

document_sections.heading: Challenging cases
document_sections.content: Complex anatomy requires experienced dissection of the UPJ to avoid vascular injury. Examples include a completely intrarenal pelvis, high ureteral insertion, a long ureteral stricture, horseshoe kidney (HSK), renal malrotation, ectopic kidney, and a duplex kidney with lower-moiety UPJO. In the largest multicenter series of complex cases described in the review, Esposito et al. recommended Anderson–Hynes pyeloplasty using da Vinci Xi. They described its adaptability to UPJ vascular anatomy in HSK or ectopic kidney, crossing vessels, lower-pole UPJO requiring preservation of upper-moiety ureteral blood supply to prevent stenosis, and fibrosis after unsuccessful open pyeloplasty. HSK has an increased incidence of UPJO associated with high ureteral insertion into the renal pelvis, the ureter’s relationship to the HSK isthmus, multiple aberrant crossing vessels, urolithiasis, and increased trauma risk. A cited multicenter HSK study by the same group reported that RALP was safe and feasible with good medium-term results: average operative time including docking was 143.5 min (range 100–205), with no conversions to laparoscopic or open surgery, no intraoperative complications, and an overall success rate of 92.8%. In adults, robot-assisted laparoscopic surgery (RALS) has been used successfully for renal stones during UPJO treatment and as primary treatment for staghorn stones. Pediatric reports indicate that pyelolithotomy and pyeloplasty for concurrent UPJO and large renal stones can safely and feasibly be performed in one operation, despite EAU guidelines recommending separate procedures for RALP and stone surgery.

document_sections.heading: Cost considerations
document_sections.content: RALP costs more than open surgery, although the difference has narrowed with time and institutional experience. Bennett et al. found in 2016 that operating-room time and supplies, together with anesthesia time, were the main contributors to the cost difference; they proposed targeting these expenses in future cost-containment efforts. A study published in 2021 found similar burdens for operating-theater use, instruments, materials, and ward recovery with open surgery and RALP, supporting RALP in a low-volume center. Removing a double-J stent added expense in that series, whereas magnetic stents reduced costs by avoiding another anesthetic procedure. Basic analyses found similar costs for robotic and conventional laparoscopic pyeloplasty, but training, maintenance, and material expenses suggest that RALP costs more than other approaches. Proposed cost-reduction measures include greater robot utilization, shorter OR turnover, and more efficient preoperative holding time. The authors argue that RALP’s direct costs, when amortization, robotic cost, maintenance, and depreciation are excluded, should not be viewed as excessive relative to other operations.

document_sections.heading: Training and learning curve
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis by Steinberg et al. found that the adult robotic prostatectomy learning curve ranged from 13 to 200 cases, averaging 77. No standardized curriculum or training protocol is yet available for pediatric robotic surgery. An open surgeon can gain RALP proficiency quickly with a proctor and an experienced team, but proctoring duration varies among surgeons, making critical self-assessment necessary. A cited study found that proficiency required at least 18 cases for LP versus 13 cases for RALP, with further improvement after 37 cases. Sorensen et al. observed initially longer RALP operative times than open-surgery times; the times became equivalent after 15–20 cases, suggesting an initial RALP learning curve of approximately that length. Esposito et al. reported a learning-curve plateau after the first 23 consecutive cases. With appropriate exposure to robotics and sufficient case volume, junior surgeons have been reported to achieve RALP expertise comparable to senior surgeons. Robotic simulation should help trainees learn instrument controls and practice operative skills, as simulation does in laparoscopy.

document_sections.heading: Future considerations
document_sections.content: Pediatric urology has adopted robotic technology increasingly, and its use is expected to continue growing; it may eventually become the gold standard for selected reconstructive procedures, particularly RALP. Existing 5 mm instruments offer limited choices, need more working space because of joint kinematics, and require a 5 mm lens that sacrifices the advantageous 3-D image. Some authors therefore favor improving 5 mm instruments or developing 3 mm instruments comparable to conventional laparoscopic tools. Future approaches may reduce the number of incisions to a single-port platform and possibly eliminate incisions. Augmented reality (AR) and augmented intelligence may be further developments in robotic surgery.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that RALP is safe and effective in children, including those with recurrent UPJO and difficult anatomy. In recurrent disease, it facilitates identification and dissection of causes of failed reconstruction, including overlooked crossing vessels, periureteral fibrosis, and ureteral stricture. It also shortens the learning curve for junior surgeons, who can attain expertise comparable to senior surgeons. High cost remains a limitation. Sharing robotic instruments across subspecialties helps contain costs but reduces opportunities to progress through the learning curve. Simulation alone does not establish proficiency; a comprehensive training program should combine simulation and mentorship. Instrument size is RALP’s main disadvantage in small children and infants. Surgeons may address it with 5 mm instruments or modified port placement, but the choice should reflect surgeon preference and the individual patient. The authors advise high-quality prospective observational studies and clinical trials of RALP in small children, a pediatric robotic training curriculum, and pediatric-specific technology and instruments before RALP reaches gold-standard status.

main_findings.description: The review reports pediatric RALP success rates across the cited literature.
main_findings.context: The article attributes this range to published pediatric RALP series.

main_findings.description: Earlier reports cited by the review described favorable RALP outcomes.
main_findings.context: This is a separate success-rate range given in the introduction for cited studies.

main_findings.description: Compared with laparoscopic pyeloplasty, the robotic approach is described as having shorter operative times, with comparable success, hospital stay and complications.
main_findings.context: The comparison appears in the review abstract without numerical estimates.

main_findings.description: Compared with open or laparoscopic pyeloplasty, RALP is described as reducing hospital stay and postoperative analgesic use.
main_findings.context: No effect estimates are provided for these comparisons.

main_findings.description: The review states that operative times for RALP, previously longer than those of other approaches, have improved, particularly with greater center volume and surgeon experience.
Most studies published from the stated year onward reported an overall operative time below the stated threshold.
main_findings.context: The review applies this statement to most studies from 2019 onward.

main_findings.description: A cited prospective multicenter comparison found both transperitoneal and retroperitoneal RALP safe and effective; retroperitoneal RALP was associated with a shorter hospital stay but a longer operative time when crossing vessels were present.
main_findings.context: Findings of the cited comparative study; the review gives no numerical estimates.

main_findings.description: A cited comparative study found that three-port RALP had success and safety similar to conventional four-port RALP, including among infants.
main_findings.context: Findings of a cited cross-sectional study using da Vinci Xi Surgical System®.

main_findings.description: Published reports indicate that robot-assisted laparoscopic single-port pyeloplasty is feasible in pediatric patients who are not infants.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to cited reports.

main_findings.description: Reports of robotic pyeloplasty without a stent describe high success and few complications relative to conventional methods, although the review notes a need for larger cohorts and longer follow-up.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to cited studies.

main_findings.description: The cited literature reports persistent or recurrent UPJO after initial pyeloplasty within the stated range.
main_findings.context: This measure concerns recurrence or persistence after initial pyeloplasty, not RALP specifically.

main_findings.description: The review describes redo RALP as effective and safe, with shorter hospitalization and fewer complications than redo open pyeloplasty and success resembling that of primary RALP.
main_findings.context: Synthesis of cited literature; no comparative estimates are supplied.

main_findings.description: A cited multicenter study of RALP in horseshoe kidney reported an average operative time that included docking.
main_findings.context: Result for the horseshoe kidney cases in the cited study.

main_findings.description: The same cited horseshoe kidney study reported the stated overall procedural success.
main_findings.context: Result for the horseshoe kidney cases in the cited study.

main_findings.description: Reports concerning children with both UPJO and large renal stones describe simultaneous pyelolithotomy and pyeloplasty in one operation as safe and feasible.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to cited pediatric reports; the review also notes that EAU guidelines recommend separate procedures.

main_findings.description: The review describes RALP as more costly than open surgery, while noting that the difference has decreased with institutional experience and time.
main_findings.context: No monetary amounts or comparative estimates are provided.

main_findings.description: Bennett et al. identified operating-room time, supplies and anesthesia time as the principal contributors to the cost difference between RALP and open pyeloplasty.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to a cited study from 2016.

main_findings.description: A cited cost study found similar burdens for theater use, instruments, materials and ward recovery with open surgery and RALP in a low-volume center; removing a double-J stent added cost, whereas magnetic stents limited costs by avoiding another anesthetic procedure.
main_findings.context: Findings attributed to a cited work published in 2021.

main_findings.description: Basic cost analyses cited by the review found similar costs for robotic and conventional laparoscopic pyeloplasty, although training, maintenance and materials can make RALP costlier than other approaches.
main_findings.context: The review distinguishes these cost assessments from direct costs that exclude amortization, robotic costs, maintenance and depreciation.

main_findings.description: A cited study reported that proficiency required fewer cases for RALP than for LP.
main_findings.context: RALP result in the cited comparison; the corresponding LP result was at least 18 cases.

main_findings.description: The same cited comparison reported continued improvement in RALP performance after additional experience.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to the cited learning-curve study.

main_findings.description: Sorensen et al. observed that RALP operative times, initially longer than those of open surgery, became equivalent after the stated number of cases.
main_findings.context: The cited authors suggested this approximated the initial RALP learning curve.

main_findings.description: Esposito et al. reported that their RALP learning curve reached a plateau after the stated consecutive cases.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to the cited study.

main_findings.description: The cited literature indicates that junior surgeons can attain RALP expertise comparable to senior surgeons when they have adequate robotic exposure and case volume.
main_findings.context: No numerical comparison is given.

notable_adverse_events: Early postoperative fever: Clavien I; no rate reported. The review defines early as < 30 days.
Early postoperative pain: Clavien I; no rate reported.
Early postoperative hematuria: Clavien I; no rate reported.
Early postoperative urinary tract infection: Clavien ≥ 2; no rate reported.
Early postoperative mild or major urinary leakage: Clavien ≥ 2; no rate reported.
Early postoperative stent migration: Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Early postoperative omental herniation: Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Early postoperative ileocecal volvulus: Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Late ipsilateral ureteral stenosis: predominantly reported as Clavien IIIb; no rate reported. The review defines late as ≥ 30 days.
Late surgical intervention for umbilical hernia: predominantly reported as Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Late J–J migration: predominantly reported as Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Late urinary leakage: predominantly reported as Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
Late stone formation: predominantly reported as Clavien IIIb; no rate reported.
In smaller children and infants, the review describes a higher risk of stent-related migration, fragmentation, infection, fever, pain and discomfort; no individual rates are reported.
The cited horseshoe kidney study reported no conversions to laparoscopy or open surgery and no intraoperative complications; event counts and rates are not stated.

subgroup_analyses: For the smallest infants, the review identifies advantages of open surgery concerning general-anesthesia duration and limitations related to robotic instrument size; it does not provide comparative estimates.

Although the review describes a consensus weight cutoff of 10–15 kg, it cites successful robotic procedures in patients under 1 year of age and in infants. It cautions that studies in younger and lighter infants are mostly retrospective.
A cited study found that 5 mm rather than 8 mm instruments improved use of the available workspace in small patients; no quantitative outcome is supplied.

For redo pyeloplasty, the review states that RALP facilitates identification and management of causes of earlier reconstruction failure, including crossing vessels, fibrosis and ureteral narrowing; no subgroup effect estimate is given.

For complex renal anatomy, a cited multicenter series favored Anderson–Hynes with da Vinci Xi because it can accommodate the anatomical challenges described; the review provides no comparative subgroup estimate.
secondary_results: The review cites prenatal hydronephrosis in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds and UPJO as its cause in up to 41% of cases.
Approximately 25% of prenatally diagnosed UPJO cases require surgery, according to a cited source.
The review cites UPJO occurrence of 1 per 1000–2000 newborns, left-kidney involvement in up to 67% of cases and bilateral disease in up to 10% of cases.
The review cites an overall success range of 90 to 100% for open Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty.
A cited comparison found similar preoperative sex distribution, laterality, renal pelvis antero-posterior diameter and affected-kidney split function between LP and RALP.

The review notes qualitative differences in reasons for secondary procedures in the cited literature: urinary leaks were more frequent after laparoscopic pyeloplasty, whereas complications associated with RPG and stent placement were reported after RALP. No rates are given.
A cited adult robotic-prostatectomy meta-analysis reported a learning-curve range of 13 to 200 cases, averaging 77; these figures do not measure pediatric RALP.
The cited LP-versus-RALP learning-curve study reported at least 18 cases to reach LP proficiency, compared with 13 cases for RALP.
